faq: How fast will I know about a problem?
Checks run every one to five minutes, depending on the tool and plan, and alerts fire as soon as a check fails twice in a row. That avoids false alarms from a single blip.
UptimeRobot, Better Stack, Grafana, Datadog or your cloud provider's own monitoring, whichever suits your size and budget. Most have free or low-cost plans, billed to you directly.
Will I get woken up at night for small things?
No. We separate urgent alerts, such as the site being down, from low-priority ones, such as a disk at 70 percent, and send them to different places. You choose what is allowed to ping a phone.
Do you respond to the alerts?
The set-up sends alerts to you or your team. We do not watch them around the clock in these packages. Ongoing response can be quoted separately as part of a monthly plan.

desc:
Server monitoring and uptime alerts watch your site, app and servers around the clock and warn the right person when something changes. Ecom Swift LLC sets up the checks, tunes the alerts so they stay useful and writes a note on what to do for each one.

## What is server monitoring and uptime alerting?

Monitoring is the automatic measuring of your systems. Uptime alerting is the part that tells a person when a measurement crosses a line. A check might request your home page every minute, a metric might track disk space, and an alert might email or message your team when either goes wrong.

Without monitoring, you learn about problems from customers. A checkout fails, a login stops working or a page crawls, and the first signal is an angry message. By then the problem has already cost trust and sales.

## Why early warning matters

Many outages start small. A disk fills slowly, memory climbs after each release, or a certificate approaches its end date. Each of these gives hours or days of warning if something is watching. Without a watcher, the first symptom is the failure itself.

Silent failures are worse. A site can return an error only on one page, or a background job can stop running while the home page looks fine. Simple external checks and error tracking catch these cases, because they test what visitors and systems actually do, not just whether a server is switched on.

## How monitoring improves reliability

Monitoring shortens the time between a problem starting and someone acting on it. That time is the largest part of most outages. It also gives your team facts. A chart showing memory growth after a release points to the cause faster than guesswork.

It supports calmer work, too. When alerts are tuned, a ping means something. When they are noisy, people mute them and miss the real one. Good alert design, with clear thresholds, the right recipients and an escalation path, is what separates helpful monitoring from background noise.

## What good monitoring includes

- Uptime checks on your main pages, login, checkout and key API endpoints.
- Response time tracking, so a slow page is noticed before it fails.
- Server health charts for CPU, memory and disk space.
- Certificate and domain expiry warnings well before the date.
- Application error tracking that groups repeated errors together.
- Central logs that can be searched during an incident.
- Alerts sent by email, Slack or Teams to named people.
- Escalation to a second person when the first does not respond.
- A public status page for customers, if you want one.
- A short playbook saying what each alert means and what to try first.

## How we set it up

We begin by asking what would hurt most if it stopped: the website, the checkout, the API, a scheduled job. We build checks around those, then add server and application metrics. We choose tools that fit your size and budget, from simple hosted uptime services to a fuller metrics and logging stack.

The tuning step matters most. We set thresholds based on how your system actually behaves, avoid alerts for things nobody can act on and group related alerts together. For each alert we write one or two lines: what it means, what to check and who to call. The Basic, Standard and Premium packages differ in the number of checks, whether you get a dashboard and chat alerts, and whether logs, error tracking and escalation are included. Alerts tell you something is wrong. They do not fix it, and response remains with your team unless you arrange otherwise.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Monitor what customers do, not only whether a server is on.
- Send each alert to a person who can act on it.
- Review thresholds after the first few weeks.
- Keep a short note beside every alert.
- Test that alerts really arrive, including after hours.

**Avoid:**
- Sending every minor event to the whole team.
- Alerting on things nobody will ever fix.
- Relying on one person's inbox as the only route.
- Leaving monitoring running on the same server it watches.
- Ignoring a repeated warning because it usually resolves itself.

## Who this is for

This service suits a small business whose website is its main sales channel and which has no one watching it at night. It suits a software team whose customers report outages before the team notices. It also suits an agency that wants one view across several client sites.

## What we need from you

Tell us your site addresses, where your servers run and who should receive alerts. Share a list of the pages or features that matter most. We never need your passwords. Access is given as a limited user on your cloud or hosting account, and monitoring tools are set up under accounts that you own.
